finding: §3's new resolved-not-stored rule mandates a refusal that cannot occur, and contradicts the change rule in the same section. It says: "a `--project` write of `all` that *uncovers* a task override of `blocking` changes the resolved value and must be refused." Under the precedence §2 states (task override > project config > built-in), a task override holding `blocking` already resolves to `blocking` before the write; a write at the *project* layer writes the lower, shadowed layer and cannot uncover anything. resolved-before == resolved-after == `blocking`, so by §3's own rule the write changes nothing and must PASS. §3's preceding paragraph says exactly that ("a write of `all` never trips it, since `all` is the default and the only value that tightens the gate"), and §7 row 13 lists "any write of `all`" among the writes that must pass. Three statements in the release, two of them added this round, and one mandates a refusal the other two forbid. Verified against internal/engine/configresolve.go:233 ResolveWorkflowLayers, where every field is pickString([]*string{taskOverride.X, project.X}, def.X) — the task layer wins unconditionally, and internal/cli/set_project.go:223 warnShadowedProjectWrites already exists precisely because a project write under a task override changes nothing. The only sink that can actually uncover a lower layer is `tp import`, which replaces the whole task-level workflow block (internal/cli/importcmd.go:158-162 — preservation runs only when the imported document carries no top-level workflow key); the layers in the example are the wrong way round.
suggestion: Delete the `--project`/`all` uncover example or replace it with the reachable one: an import whose document carries a `workflow` key drops a task-level `all` and uncovers a project-level `blocking`, which changes the resolved value and must be refused. Then reconcile the two sentences that currently say a write of `all` never trips the fence — under the change rule that is true for `tp set` and its `--project` form, and false for `tp import`, which can change the resolved value without naming the field at all.

finding: §7 was rewritten this round as a derivation table whose stated purpose is that "a decision that changes and leaves its row untouched is visible", and it already fails on §3's newest decision. §3's paragraph "**\"Resolved\" means resolved, not stored at the written layer**" carries two normative cases — a `--project` write of `blocking` under a task override of `all` must PASS, and a write that uncovers a task-level `blocking` must be REFUSED — and neither has a row. Row 12 derives from "§3 *the change rule*" and covers only refusals of a write of `blocking`; row 13 derives from the same and lists "any write of `all`" and "an import carrying an already-resolved `blocking` forward" as the passes. The one case that discriminates a resolved-scoped fence from a fence scoped to the written layer — writing `blocking` at the project layer under a task `all` — appears in no row, so an implementation comparing the value written at its own layer instead of the resolved value passes all nineteen rows. The column introduced to make an unmaintained row visible did not make this one visible on the round it was introduced.
suggestion: Add a row deriving from "§3 *resolved, not stored*": a `--project` write of `blocking` under a task override of `all` exits 0 under TP_UNATTENDED=1, falsifying input "a fence comparing the value written at its own layer rather than the resolved value". Add the mirror refusal row once §3's uncover case is restated on a reachable sink, and drop or qualify "any write of `all`" in row 13 so it does not contradict that paragraph.

finding: Round 10 tightened §4's emission condition and stranded the paragraph and the test that depend on the old one. Round 9's snapshot (spec/.tp-review/0.37.0/snapshot-round-9.md:165) reads "Emitted when the round has at least one non-`PASS` row"; round 10 reads "Emitted when the merged round would be clean under the resolved policy *and* holds at least one non-`PASS` row". Under §2 a round is clean under `blocking` only when no non-`PASS` row carries a blocking severity, and an unrecognised severity IS blocking. So on every round where `by_severity` is emitted, `error` == 0 and `unrecognised` == 0 by construction; under `all` the key never appears at all. That makes §4's own claim — "`error` + `unrecognised` sums the round's blocking rows and the two sections cannot drift apart" — the identity 0 == 0, which can detect no drift, and it makes §7 row 17 unwritable: its fixture "carrying all four unrecognised shapes" is by definition not clean under `blocking`, so `by_severity` is absent and there are no buckets to sum. Only `warning` and `info` can ever be non-zero in an emitted breakdown. This is the failure §7's preamble says round 9 measured — "four tests demanding the implementation the sections had just rejected" — reappearing on the round the derivation column was added to prevent it.
suggestion: Pick one. Either keep the clean-gated emission and cut the blocking-row-sum claim and row 17 — the emitted breakdown is a warning/info breakdown and saying so is honest — or state that `by_severity` is also emitted on an unclean round so the invariant has a population, which reopens the "key on every round that has any finding" case round 10 just closed. Either way row 17's falsifying input must name a fixture the emission condition can reach.

finding: The change rule closes the two deadlocks the table names and leaves a third one reachable, through the very configuration §3 declares legal. §3 says a `--project` write of `blocking` under a task override of `all` "changes nothing an audit will read, and must pass" — so a project may legitimately end up with project `blocking` under task `all`. Now run Workflow A step 6 in that project. `tp import` carries the existing workflow block forward only when the imported document has NO top-level workflow key (internal/cli/importcmd.go:158 `!importedHasWorkflowKey(trimmed)`); a decomposer's tasks.json that carries `"workflow": {}` — the exact shape this repository's own v0.26.0 migration wrote into its task files — skips preservation, so `tf.Workflow` becomes empty, the task-level `all` is dropped, and the project's `blocking` becomes the resolved value. resolved-before `all`, resolved-after `blocking`: the change rule refuses it. The import never mentions `audit_converge_on`, the unit cannot make it pass by editing the document (adding the field back is itself a write the fence must judge), and Workflow A step 6 deadlocks under `tp run` for an opt-in project — the same failure round 9 reported against the value-scoped fence, arriving by a different route the new table does not list.
suggestion: Add a fourth row to §3's table for it, and decide the case: either an import that changes the resolved value only by dropping a shadowing layer is exempt (the project layer was operator-approved, so nothing new is being approved by a unit), or `tp import` must preserve a task-level `audit_converge_on` across a workflow-block replacement the way it preserves the whole block today. Whichever is chosen, §7 needs the row, since row 13's "an import carrying an already-resolved `blocking` forward" does not cover an import that changes the resolved value to `blocking` by removing an override.

finding: §4's bucket rule reverses round 9's decision in the direction the section says it exists to prevent. Round 9 (snapshot-round-9.md:171-176): "A severity that is a string outside the enum keys on that string. A severity that is JSON `null`, absent, or not a string at all keys on **`unrecognised`**" — an unknown string stayed visible. Round 10 folds all four shapes into `unrecognised`, justified by the sum invariant that finding 3 above shows is vacuous under the new emission condition. The cost is the one diagnostic the breakdown could have carried: a typo'd or mis-cased severity (`Error`, `blocker`, `errror`) is exactly the row an operator on `blocking` must find and fix, because §2's fail-closed rule silently makes it blocking, and after round 10 the breakdown no longer names it. "The point is that nothing hides" is now false for the shape most likely to occur, and the reason given for hiding it no longer holds.
suggestion: Restore round 9's split — enum severities and any other string key on themselves, `null`/absent/non-string on `unrecognised` — and if the sum invariant is kept, phrase it as "`error` plus every non-enum bucket" rather than as a two-term sum. That keeps §2's fail-closed population summable without erasing which literal produced it.

finding: §2's `next_action` decision, strengthened this round, ships the information §6 Non-Goal 4 defers, on the surface Non-Goal 4 defers it from. §2 now requires that under `blocking` the recommendation "states that the phase may proceed and names how many non-`PASS` rows were accepted", and `next_action` is emitted by both audit sinks — internal/cli/audit_record.go:125 (`--record`) and :391 (`--status`). §6 Non-Goal 4 defers "`nonblocking_open` on `--record` and `--status`" because "four places pin its absence there by name". The four guards pin a key, so nothing reddens; but the accepted-open count is now delivered on `--record` and `--status` regardless, as a substring instead of a field. The deferral therefore defers the shape and not the information, and an agent parsing the count out of prose is worse off than one reading a key — which is the AX argument the deferral was resting on.
suggestion: Say so in Non-Goal 4: what is deferred is the `nonblocking_open` key, not the fact, because §2 puts the count in `next_action`'s text on the same two commands. If that reads as an admission the key should just ship, that is the honest reading and belongs in §6 rather than being left for a decomposer to notice.

finding: "The comparison is resolved-before against resolved-after, at every sink" does not say which task file the import sink resolves against, and the one reusable helper resolves the wrong one. `tp import` writes `targetPath`, derived from `tf.Spec` (internal/cli/importcmd.go:141-143), while the existing fence's resolver, `resolvedWorkflowForFence` (internal/cli/unattended.go:90-98), reads `engine.DiscoverTaskFile(".", flagFile)` — the active task file recorded in `.tp/local.json`. In this repository those routinely differ: `tp use` points `active` at the cycle in flight while a new spec's tasks are imported to a different `<base>.tasks.json`. A fence copying the existing helper would compare the resolved value of a task file the import is not writing, and would both refuse legal imports and pass the refusable one. The `tp set --workflow` sink has the mirror of the same gap: it calls `fenceWorkflowWrite` during argument parsing, before `engine.WithFileLock(taskFilePath, ...)` at line 445, so resolved-before is read outside the lock that guards the write.
suggestion: State at §3 that each sink resolves against the file it is about to write — `targetPath` for `tp import`, the discovered task file for `tp set --workflow`, the project config plus that file for the `--project` form — and that the import comparison is made inside the write lock, after the §9.3 workflow-preservation step has decided what `tf.Workflow` will be. Give §7 row 12's import assertion a fixture where the active task file and the import target differ, or the assertion passes on a fence reading either one.

finding: Row 7 ("§2 table | `error` blocks") has an em dash in "the input that makes it fail". The table's whole argument is that the derivation and the falsifying input are what keep a row honest — §7's preamble measures round 9's list as "12 [writable] and 8 [discriminating]" and calls the column the fix. A row with no falsifying input is a row that certifies itself, which is the state the column was added to make visible, and it is visible here only as punctuation.
suggestion: Fill it: "a predicate that treats `error` as advisory", or "a `blocking` predicate that returns clean for any round, which rows 5 and 6 also pass". If no input can discriminate row 7 from rows 5 and 6, fold it into them rather than carrying a row the column cannot support.
